motion: Do we need God for morality?

items.currentText: Clearly isolated the gap between descriptive scientific facts and categorical prescriptions.
items.lockedProposition: Descriptions supplied by nature and science do not themselves yield moral prescriptions about what anyone should do.

items.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Ferrer articulates the descriptive normative gap with precision and correctly observes that scientific accounts of consequences do not independently establish which ends agents categorically should adopt. Principal limitation: Showing that bare descriptions lack prescriptions does not demonstrate that God supplies the missing normativity because the argument leaves unexplained how facts about divine existence or character cross the same inferential boundary. Live burden: He must provide an additional normative principle connecting divine nature to human obligation and defend that principle without presupposing the categorical authority whose source remains disputed.

items.currentText: Correctly distinguished moral truth from sincere desire and belief about goodness.
items.lockedProposition: A desire and belief concerning good can constitute morality only if good actually exists independently of those attitudes.

items.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The response precisely isolates the truth-dependent presupposition within the opposing formula, distinguishing desire-and-belief sincerity from whether the desired object independently qualifies as genuinely good. Principal limitation: The excerpt repeatedly asserts that good must antecedently exist, yet supplies neither an account of independent goodness nor an inference establishing that attitude-independent moral reality requires God specifically. Live burden: The argument must demonstrate why nontheistic moral facts cannot furnish the demanded truth conditions, while connecting divine existence to goodness without circularly presupposing the very metaphysical dependence under dispute.
